corrected_value.authors: Kelly, W. P., & Tomhave, W. K.
corrected_value.title: A study of math anxiety/math avoidance in preservice elementary teachers.

decision.quote: The current study replicated the finding that female elementary school teachers have a higher level of math anxiety in relation to female students from other fields (【10†Hembree, 1990】; 【26†Kelly & Tomhave, 1985】; 【32†Szczygieł & Cipora, 2016】). On average, math anxiety was higher in pre-service and in-service female elementary school teachers as compared to female university students from various fields ranging from the sciences to the humanities.
decision.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent. In the Introduction (lines 35, 45) and Discussion (lines 226, 229, 242), the authors explicitly frame their comparison of elementary school teachers' math anxiety against reference students from other fields (and between female and male teachers) as replicating Kelly and Tomhave (1985), testing this in new German and Belgian samples (Results lines 103-108). The reference list confirms the primary empirical article in The Arithmetic Teacher, 32(5), 51-53 (doi:10.5951/AT.32.5.0051). Shipped row 2178 is Hembree (1990), a meta-analysis, and sibling target 2 is Szczygieł and Cipora (2016), an independent Polish primary study; neither is an alternate report of Kelly and Tomhave (1985).

On average, math anxiety was higher in pre-service and in-service female elementary school teachers as compared to female university students from various fields ranging from the sciences to the humanities.
decision.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent. The Introduction (line 44) highlights Szczygieł and Cipora's (2016) specific finding that female pre-service elementary school teachers express higher math anxiety than female students from other fields, Results (lines 106-108) directly tests this comparison between female elementary school teachers and female university students from other fields (t(818) = 2.28, p = .023), and Discussion (line 229) explicitly states that the current study replicated this finding of Szczygieł and Cipora (2016). The reference list (line 362) verifies the primary study in Problemy Wczesnej Edukacji, 2(33), 89-101 (doi:10.5604/01.3001.0009.4827). It is distinct from shipped row 2178 (Hembree, 1990 meta-analysis) and sibling target 1 (Kelly & Tomhave, 1985).

corrected_value.title: Environmental disorder leads to self-regulatory failure.

decision.quote: All Order-Disorder comparisons were not significant also in the case of the executive functioning measures (see Table 1 ). Results remained unchanged after removing outliers scores 3 SD away from the mean ( n = 5). Ancillary Analysis A series of additional analyses were conducted to test differences between task rotations. We also compared the effect of experimental conditions only considering the rotations that most closely resembled the task order in Vohs et al. (2013) and Chae and Zhu (2014) .
decision.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent. In addition to testing Vohs et al.'s (2013) disorder-creativity effect (shipped row 2478), this paper tests whether workspace disorder impairs executive functioning as reported by Chae and Zhu (2014). In Results (Table 1 and Ancillary Analysis), the authors compare Order vs. Disorder conditions on multiple executive control measures, including task-order rotations aligned specifically with Chae and Zhu (2014), and in Discussion they directly contrast their null executive-functioning results and larger sample size (n = 50 per group vs. 20-25) with Chae and Zhu (2014). The reference list (lines 5-6) confirms the identity (Journal of Consumer Research, 40, 1203-1218, doi:10.1086/674547), which is an independent study from shipped row 2478 (Vohs et al., 2013).

corrected_value.title: Which cognitive abilities underlie computational thinking? Criterion validity of the computational thinking test.

decision.quote:
Concerning the replication part of our project, our results support the view that CT is
underpinned by reasoning, as assessed by figural reasoning, and spatial abilities, as

decision.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent. This pre-registered replication study explicitly re-tests Román-González, Pérez-González, and Jiménez-Fernández (2017) (Computers in Human Behavior, 72, 678-691, doi:10.1016/j.chb.2016.08.047) on the cognitive predictors (reasoning, spatial visualization, and arithmetic) and gender differences in Computational Thinking test performance in a new sample of 132 Austrian 7th-8th grade students. Shipped row 797 is a different paper—Román-González, Pérez-González, Moreno-León, and Robles (2018) on non-cognitive factors (Computers in Human Behavior, 80, 441-459, doi:10.1016/j.chb.2017.09.030)—which is cited only once as background at line 780 and listed separately in the bibliography (lines 1109-1111).
